claims.text: The starting material is a homogenized, single-phase, equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi solid-solution alloy with controlled grain size and minimal secondary phases.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has relatively low hardness and strength.
Ti lowers the effective Peierls barrier in nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti weakens solute–dislocation interactions in nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The Ti-induced lattice state reduces the effective resistance to dislocation motion.
Ti incorporation changes lattice parameters and local stacking-fault energies in a way that enhances dislocation mobility.
Ti incorporation minimizes dislocation pinning in the solid solution.
Substitutional Ti produces only moderate lattice distortion in the CoCrFeNi matrix.
The moderate lattice distortion creates fewer effective solute-pinning points than would otherwise be expected.
Reduced solute pinning shifts deformation away from conventional forest hardening and increases the contribution of grain-boundary processes.
More facile dislocation glide and greater grain-boundary-mediated plasticity cause the relatively low hardness and strength.
At comparable grain size and structural state, equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will have lower yield strength than a Ti-reduced or Ti-depleted control.
At comparable grain size and structural state, equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will have lower hardness than a Ti-reduced or Ti-depleted control.
In-situ TEM will show greater dislocation mobility in the Ti-containing alloy than in the Ti-reduced control.
In-situ observations will show preferential grain-boundary sliding or activation in the Ti-containing alloy.
The proposed mechanism is limited to homogenized, single-phase alloys with comparable grain size and minimal secondary phases under room-temperature quasi-static loading.
Behavior under high-temperature or high-strain-rate loading may differ from the proposed room-temperature quasi-static behavior.
